idiom_name: explicit release() in finally; using + Symbol.dispose as the declarative form
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no destructors, so the hand-back is an explicit call: acquire, then try { ... } finally { r.release(); }, or - where runtime and toolchain support explicit resource management - declare using r = pool.acquire(). Symbol.dispose is the well-known symbol the using declaration looks up on the initializer to call when the variable goes out of scope (MDN), so a lending wrapper implements [Symbol.dispose]() as its hand-back and works with both styles; use Symbol.asyncDispose for asynchronous returns. The idiomatic replacement for the C++ return type is a factory returning an object whose documented release is the only path back to the owner.
pitfalls: Relying on garbage collection to return the resource starves the pool: dropping a reference does not call release, so the free list never sees the object again.
An async function that acquires before its first await and throws can skip a release placed after the await; keep the hand-back in finally, or use using with Symbol.asyncDispose.
using requires runtime support - Symbol.dispose and DisposableStack are often polyfilled - so mixed deployments silently fall back to try/finally discipline.
